content.title: The best Irish films of all time: the definitive top 30
content.text: As the success of An Cailín Ciúin and The Banshees of Inisherin shows, our national cinema has never been in better shape. Here is our list of our very best movies, as voted by 30 film-makers and criticsWhat makes our favourite films our favourite films? Nostalgia? Beloved stars? Stunning cinematography? Heart-rending scenes and compelling stories?It can be a subjective business, which is why we cast our net wide and deep for our selection of the 30 best Irish feature films. It was chosen by a distinguished panel of film-makers, producers, critics, broadcasters, programmers, distributors and festival directors who are well placed to assess the state of our national cinema.A list of more than 70 exceptional Irish films was whittled down to a final list of 30.If you wanted a barometer for the state of Irish cinema, it’s worth noting that half of the films on our list were made in the last 20 years. There had always been trailblazers, of course: maverick film-makers such as Neil Jordan and Jim Sheridan who bucked the odds to create big films that made an international splash. But until the early 2000s, Ireland was such a tough and unyielding environment for film-makers that the late Irish Times critic Michael Dwyer used to talk of the “extra star” Irish movies should be awarded simply for getting made.But that time is well and truly past. If Jordan and Sheridan proved that Irish movie-makers could compete with the best, the building blocks of a real domestic film industry did not emerge until the early 2000s. And in a way, one can talk about Irish cinema before and after Adam & Paul.Lenny Abrahamson and Mark O’Halloran’s ambitious and poetic tale of two Dublin drug addicts marked a decisive departure from the wordy theatricality that had tended (with honourable exceptions) to afflict Irish cinema to that point. A confident new generation of Irish directors and writers was emerging that were less influenced by Irish theatre than by Hollywood films.John Carney, Pat Collins, Nora Twomey and Tomm Moore at Cartoon Saloon, Emer Reynolds and Carmel Winters among others began making films that had more in common with European cinema traditions. A boom was happening, a modest one perhaps, with budgets to match, but a proliferation of talent meant that good Irish films were no longer rare and wonderful events.Read moreThere is no room on our list, unfortunately, for any of the fine horror films that have emerged from these shores over the last decade or so, though there might have been, because some of them — Lee Cronin’s The Hole in the Ground for example — are very good.In terms of defining what constitutes an applicable film, An Cailín Ciúin couldn’t be more Irish if it tried — written and directed by an Irishman, conducted as Gaeilge by an all-Irish cast. But with other supposedly Irish films, the waters become muddy. Barry Lyndon, for example, which was voted greatest Irish film of all time by another newspaper, was written, directed and produced by an American, Stanley Kubrick, using a mainly non-Irish cast.Odd Man Out was a British-produced film directed by an Englishman, Carol Reed. Calling The Quiet Man an Irish film seems equally perverse, as does claiming the work of the great Yorgos Lanthimos simply because Element Pictures co-produce his films.Barry Lyndon does make our list, because our judges, who know what they’re doing, decided to claim it (many scenes were shot here), but in the main, these are properly Irish films, created and realised by Irish talent. And the list forms a road map of Irish cinema’s development over the last 60 years or so, from the daring transgressions of Peter Lennon’s Rocky Road to Dublin to the incisive dramas and documentaries of Pat Murphy and Margo Harkin, the Oscar heroics of Jordan and Sheridan and the dawn of a truly prolific national cinema.Looking at the recent success of An Cailín Ciúin and Banshees of Inisherin makes you wonder what might be achieved over the next 10 years. I can’t wait to find out.30 Hush-a-bye-Baby (1989)As raw and powerful as the day it was released, Margo Harkin’s unflinching and insightful drama follows the fortunes of Goretti (Emer McCourt), a teenage Derry girl who is involved in a tentative relationship with Ciarán, an Irish speaker and ardent republican. When he is arrested for suspected membership of the IRA, Goretti begins to feel ill and realises to her horror that she is pregnant. Overcome with terror, she hides her condition from her family and her best friends Dinky, Sinéad and Majella and removes herself to the Donegal Gaeltacht to improve her Irish.Ciarán, she reckons, will understand, but when she finally tells him, he reacts with cruel indifference, leading Goretti to consider desperate measures. McCourt is superb in the leading role, and Sinéad O’Connor is a wonderfully ethereal presence as Goretti’s friend Sinéad. A powerful film, and a brave one, especially for its time.Mebh and Robyn in Wolfwalkers29 Wolfwalkers (2020)The hardest thing for Kilkenny animation titans Cartoon Saloon must be matching their own high standards, but in Wolfwalkers they managed to surpass them. More ambitious visually than previous films including The Secret of Kells and Song of the Sea, Wolfwalkers is set in 17th century Ireland, where England’s invading Lord Protector has established himself in a walled town. Wolves lurk in the forests around, and Cromwell has brought a master hunter called Bill Goodfellowe (voiced by Sean Bean) to wipe them out.As a result, Goodfellowe’s daughter Robyn (Honor Kneafsey) is left to her own devices, and one day she gets lost in the forest and meets a strange girl called Mebh (Eva Whittaker). She is a Wolfwalker, an ancient tribe said to commune with wolves and transform into them at night, and soon Robyn is caught between two very different worlds. The film’s animation is gorgeous, cleverly contrasting the boxy lines of the walled town with the vibrant wildness of the wilderness the invader is so keen to expunge.Caitriona Balfe, Jamie Dornan, Judi Dench, Jude Hill and Lewis McAskie in Belfast. Photo: Rob Youngson28 Belfast (2021)Kenneth Branagh is perhaps the plummiest Shakespearean actor of his generation, but once he spoke with a very different voice. Born in Belfast in 1960, he left the city at the age of nine as a consequence of the Troubles, which devastated the working-class Protestant enclave from which his family hailed. In this sumptuous drama, filmed mainly in crisp black and white, Branagh evokes the fleeting intimacy of his Northern Irish childhood, which is about to be shattered by riots, bombs and cross-community gangsterism.Buddy (the excellent Jude Hill) is a bright and lively nine-year-old who lives with his parents (Jamie Dornan and Caitríona Balfe) and older brother in the cramped but cosy working-class streets of north Belfast. Civil rights marches, and the furious response of the Orange state, have led to wide unrest. The onset of the Troubles leads his family to make a fateful and difficult decision. Ciarán Hinds and Judi Dench play Buddy’s doting grandparents in this irresistible and heartfelt film.27 Intermission (2003)“A likeable film about nasty people” was how American critic Richard Roeper described Intermission, and that pretty much sums it up. And while it was accused in its day of being sub-Tarantino, John Crowley and Mark O’Rowe’s swaggering comic crime caper is much more original than that. In one of Irish cinema’s most memorable openings, petty thief Lehiff (Colin Farrell) flirts with a young shop cashier (Kerry Condon), then punches her in the face and robs the till.Lehiff is high on the hit list of Jerry Lynch (Colm Meaney) a deeply unpleasant garda detective who believes it is his divine mission to drive the “scumbags” off Dublin’s streets. A galaxy of supporting characters includes warring couple John and Deirdre (Cillian Murphy and Kelly Macdonald), luckless Romeo Oscar (David Wilmot), and an odious small boy with a talent for causing chaos. Intermission is of its time perhaps, but full of memorable moments.26 Maeve (1981)Pat Murphy’s remarkable 1980s drama managed to be both dreamlike and sternly realistic at once. Shot on the fly on the streets of Belfast, it tells the story of Maeve Sweeney (Mary Jackson), a young woman from a nationalist background who returns to Northern Ireland after studying in London just as the Troubles reach their height. As she reckons with her past, she feels alienated by everything around her, from the RUC who once beat her to the arrogant, swaggering British soldiers to the sexist dogmatism of the IRA.Her boyfriend Liam (John Keegan) is a member, and haughtily explains that “I represent the women here more than you do”. Bríd Brennan plays her sister Róisín, and Murphy’s brilliant feature moves fluently back and forth in time to give us a fuller picture of Maeve’s turbulent life.‘Superb central performances from Donal McCann, Ciarán Hinds and Saskia Reeves capture a sparse, Bible-bound Ulster. Director Thaddeus O’Sullivan throws light into dark corners’ Seán Rocks on December BrideCiarán Hinds and Saskia Reeves in December Bride25 December Bride (1990)A boldly original Irish film based on a novel by northern novelist Sam Hanna Bell, Thaddeus O’Sullivan’s stately and absorbing drama stars Saskia Reeves as Sarah Gilmartin, a single-minded young woman whose contempt for convention causes ructions in a small Ulster town. It’s 1909, and Sarah arrives with her mother to work as housekeeper for a widower and his two grown sons. Scandalised by the family’s laissez-faire attitude to church-going, the mother quickly departs, but Sarah settles right in, and begins a relationship with the younger brother Frank (Ciarán Hinds).Before you know it, older brother Hamilton (Donal McCann) has joined in, and when Sarah falls pregnant, she refuses to marry either sibling or reveal who the father is. She emerges as something of a counterculture heroine in this thought-provoking drama.Jack Reynor and Ferdia Walsh-Peelo in Sing Street24 Sing Street (2016)John Carney has made a number of fine films, but while Once might be the best known, Sing Street is more substantial and likeable. Loosely based on Carney’s youth, the musical drama follows the fortunes of Conor Lalor (Ferdia Walsh-Peelo), who is not best pleased when his father pulls him out of an exclusive private school and sends him to Synge Street, the inner-city Christian Brothers’ school. Conor thinks it’s the end of the world but in fact it’s a new beginning, as he joins forces with like-minded teens to form a band.It’s all being done to impress a girl of course, the grand and ethereal Raphina (Lucy Boynton), who claims she’s a model and plans to move to London. Don Wycherley gives an amusing turn as an apoplectic Christian Brother and Jack Reynor is very good as Conor’s laconic, pot-smoking older brother. All in all, a heartwarming film.23 His & Hers (2009)In his debut feature, Portarlington film-maker Ken Wardrop made good on the promise of his short documentaries with an absorbing exploration of Irish womanhood. Filming with a small crew in the heart of the midlands, he asks females from the age of five or six to 90 to discuss the men in their lives, from brothers and fathers to husbands and sons. His & Hers builds an extraordinary cumulative power that reaches its climax in the recollections of elderly ladies including Wardrop’s own mother about coping with the death of the men they loved.Wardrop shoots all of this simply and directly, with a fixed camera: the faces and the personalities provide the fireworks, though he often situates his subjects near homely props that give hints as to their deeper stories.Funny, profound and lovely to look at, Wardrop’s film presents an intriguing kaleidoscope of the Irish female experience.‘This stunning work from Pat Murphy is a historical reclamation of the story of Robert Emmett’s so-called housekeeper, Anne Devlin. Based intensely on Anne’s prison writing, it’s beautifully shot, with that famous tableau of the noble Bríd Brennan standing up in a horse and cart as she’s surrounded by redcoats’ Margo Harkin on Anne Devlin22 Anne Devlin (1984)The second Pat Murphy film to make our list, this eloquent historical drama tells the story of Anne Devlin, who conspired with Robert Emmett to overthrow British rule in Ireland. Incensed by the brutal repression of the 1798 rising, Anne (Bríd Brennan) becomes an active insurrectionist, and introduces Emmett to her Wicklow cousin Michael Dwyer, who promises to lead a rebellion from the mountains if Emmett can supply him with guns.While posing as Emmett’s housekeeper, Anne conspired in the planning of the 1803 rebellion, which failed miserably but would become a beacon of hope for republicans.Making a film in Ireland in the mid-1980s was no joke, but with Thaddeus O’Sullivan as her cinematographer, Murphy managed to make something pretty special. “With Anne Devlin’s journal,” she said afterwards, “I wanted to tell a story that was like a ballad.” She did just that.Richard Dormer (centre) as Terri in Good Vibrations21 Good Vibrations (2012)Lisa Barros D’Sa’s wryly amusing drama is set in Northern Ireland at the start of the Troubles and tells the rousing tale of Terri Hooley. A music-obsessed hippie, Terri (Richard Dormer) decides to open a record shop in downtown Belfast at a time when retailers were deserting it in droves.In the film’s most pivotal scene, Terri has a eureka moment after stumbling into a raucous gig by a young punk outfit called the Outcasts. Gripped by one of his characteristic enthusiasms, he sets up a record label to promote singles by bands such as the Outcasts and Rudi, and then one day, the Undertones walk into his shop and present him with a demo.Good Vibrations brilliantly evokes the edgy paranoia of ’70s Belfast, and gives a sense of what was going on in the background without getting bogged down in history. And Dormer is exceptionally good as the charming and eternally optimistic Hooley.20 In America (2002)Co-written with his daughters Naomi and Kirsten, and by some distance Jim Sheridan’s most personal film, In America is based on his family’s experiences in New York in the early 1980s. Paddy Considine plays struggling Irish actor Johnny Sullivan, who finds a home in a ramshackle Hell’s Kitchen tenement for his wife Sarah (Samantha Morton) and their two young daughters. Johnny, a Catholic, has begun to question his faith following his young son’s death, but unlikely friendships blossom in a building full of transvestites and drug addicts.In one of his best screen performances, Djimon Hounsou gives a heartwarming portrayal of Mateo, a HIV-positive neighbour who is befriended by Johnny’s daughters, and has a crucial role to play. A moving and underrated film.Saoirse Ronan and Emory Cohen in Brooklyn 19 Brooklyn (2015)A charming melodrama based on Colm Tóibín’s bestselling novel, Brooklyn is set in the 1950s and stars Saoirse Ronan as Eilis Lacey, a young Wexford woman who lives with her mother and works part-time in a local shop. But her dreams are big, and a chance arises to travel across the Atlantic and start a new life in New York.With the help of a priest, she finds a home in a Brooklyn boarding house run by a prim Irish landlady (a hilarious Julie Walters), and a job at a downtown department store.She falls in love with an Italian-American plumber called Tony, but also has feelings for a young man back home. And when Eilis hears that her sister has died suddenly, she has a big decision to make.Lushly directed by John Crowley from a witty script by Nick Hornby, Brooklyn is light enough, but Ronan’s assured and subtle performance holds the whole thing together beautifully.Kelly O'Neill and Shane Curry in Kisses18 Kisses (2008)Lance Daly’s ambitious Famine drama Black ’47 may not have made our list, but this soulful odyssey deservedly has, and it’s the visual flair and originality of Kisses that most impresses. A kind of Homeric epic set in the commonplace modern day, it stars Kelly O’Neill as Kylie and Shane Curry as Dylan — two troubled pre-teens who learn hard lessons on a night-time journey across Dublin.Kylie is being abused by a relative, and Dylan faces regular beatings from his father, but one winter’s day they escape their west Dublin estate and hop aboard a passing barge that takes them to the heart of the city.Kylie has money and they buy new clothes before exploring the glitzy heart of Dublin by night. They think it’s magical, but there are monsters in the wings, and the pair soon learn that the world is even harsher than they thought.Daly’s story is slender, but he handles it beautifully, helped by the wonderfully unaffected performances of his young leads.‘A wonderful film from a director [Stephen Frears] whose work I really love. It’s funny and moving and perfectly captures our Irish sense of humour, stoicism and occasional propensity to bad behaviour’ Lisa Mulcahy on The Snapper Sharon Curley (Tina Kellegher) with her baby in The Snapper17 The Snapper (1993)Arguably the most authentic of the Roddy Doyle adaptations, Stephen Frears’ charming low-budget TV film features a barnstorming performance from Colm Meaney. He is Dessie Curley, a northside working-class Dub who’s horrified when he discovers that his daughter Sharon is pregnant.She claims the father is a Spanish sailor, but meanwhile George Burgess, her best friend’s father, has left his wife. It’s only a matter of time before the hot-headed Dessie finds out what’s really going on, and when he does, everyone had better watch out.Tina Kellegher is Sharon, Pat Laffan is George and a young Brendan Gleeson gives a very touching turn as Dessie’s friend Lester. Perhaps the film that best catches our capital city’s salty sense of humour.Forest Whitaker and Stephen Rea in The Crying Game16 The Crying Game (1992)One of the best films of 1992, Neil Jordan’s searingly original thriller used the Troubles as a backdrop for a fascinating exploration of identity. Taciturn IRA man Fergus (Stephen Rea) forms a bond with a British soldier called Jody (Forest Whitaker) whom his unit has kidnapped. When Jody dies, Fergus is racked with guilt, and goes to London to fulfil a promise he made to Jody that he would visit his girlfriend, Dil (Jaye Davidson). Fergus falls in love with her, but feels the urge to confess his role in Jody’s death to Dil, who has even bigger surprises in store.The film’s big twist was a major talking point on its release, but more interesting was the idea of role-playing, and the imposed restrictions of gender and nationality. Rea has rarely been better playing a character who in his time and place has become a terrorist, but might have been someone very different.15 Barry Lyndon (1975)Though it won best Irish film in another newspaper’s poll, Barry Lyndon’s credentials in that regard seem problematic. Written and directed by an American, Stanley Kubrick, the sumptuous period drama was only partly shot here (thanks to an IRA death threat), and does not feature many Irish players. But it is a great film, our jury voted for it, and they know best.Ryan O’Neal is Redmond Barry, the 18th-century rake, gambler and social climber who attaches himself to a noble Englishwoman, Lady Lyndon (Marisa Berenson) to claim her husband’s title. He becomes Barry Lyndon, but disaster and misfortune await.Contemporary audiences complained about the film’s length and stately pacing, but time has been kind to Kubrick’s epic. Cinematographer John Alcott used super-fast 50mm lenses to shoot interior scenes lit only by candlelight, and the results were sensational.Michael Fassbender as Bobby Sands in Hunger 14 Hunger (2008)Steve McQueen’s hard-hitting drama did not sugarcoat the appalling conditions that prevailed inside the Maze Prison in the early 1980s, when republican prisoners demanding political status dressed themselves in blankets, refused to wash and smeared their cell walls with excrement. Grim stuff, but when a piece of art is good enough, it somehow transcends the horror and makes the unwatchable bearable. In a star-making performance, Michael Fassbender is Bobby Sands, the charismatic west Belfast IRA man who leads his colleagues on a dreadful hunger strike.Londoner McQueen was only 11 when Sands died, and perhaps that distance in time and location helped him approach this subject with a fresh and curious eye. The film is visually remarkable, arguably the best that’s ever been made about the Troubles. Fassbender summons extraordinary intensity in his portrayal of Sands, especially during a 20-minute encounter with Liam Cunningham’s anguished priest.‘Peter Lennon’s excoriating portrait of a country that followed the passion and fire of revolution by merely swapping one form of subservience for another is all the more effective for its shrewd approach. While it remains an astonishing document of the nascent republic, it also represents opportunities missed, and is crying out for a contemporary companion piece’ Kevin Coyne on Rocky Road to DublinSmokers in the 1967 documentary The Rocky Road to Dublin13 Rocky Road to Dublin (1967)Notoriously the last film shown at Cannes in 1968 before Truffaut and Godard suspended the festival in sympathy with striking Parisian students, Peter Lennon’s freewheeling documentary offered a fascinating glimpse into the repressive Ireland of that time. While most other western democracies were experiencing the heady thrill of youth revolt, Ireland was still stifled by the dead hand of the Catholic Church, best embodied in Lennon’s film by the Nosferatu stylings of John Charles McQuaid.Filming on the fly in pubs and dance halls, Croke Park and — most revealingly — at a tennis club dance, Lennon showed how generations of repression had left Ireland’s youth awkward and unsure of themselves in terms of self-expression. And as for the position of women, we watch with interest as three male students talk rudely over a lone female every time she tries to join in. What foreign audiences must have thought watching all this, one can only imagine, but change was coming, and within a decade, Ireland would be transformed.12 The Farthest (2017)One of the standout films of 2017, Emer Reynolds’ enthralling documentary told in bold terms the story of Voyager I, a Nasa space probe launched in 1977 with the noble aim of introducing ourselves to extraterrestrials. Using technology less sophisticated than a modern car key fob, scientists created a flying orb that was both cultural repository and a close observer of everything it passed.On board, in case the probe might ever be found by intelligent aliens, is a golden disc containing classic literature, music from Mozart and Chuck Berry, and more poignantly the sound of whale song and waves crashing on a shore. Over the decades, magnificent photos of Saturn, Jupiter and their moons have been beamed back by the little war horse, which is now believed to have entered interstellar space. As one scientist says, Voyager “may, in the long run, be the only evidence that we ever existed”. There’s a sobering thought.Brendan Gleeson in The Banshees of Inisherin11 The Banshees of Inisherin (2022)Set on a remote Atlantic island during the Civil War, Martin McDonagh’s Banshees of Inisherin tells a minor tragedy in a major key. Fiddler and amateur philosopher Colm (Brendan Gleeson) and amiable small farmer Pádraic (Colin Farrell) have been friends for years, until one day Colm decides he has had enough. “I don’t like you any more,” he tells a crestfallen Pádraic, before explaining that he feels the hand of death on his shoulder and wants to spend his remaining days writing music that will outlive him. And when Pádraic doesn’t get the message, Colm issues a bizarre threat: every time Pádraic talks to him, he’ll cut off one of his own fingers.Which sounds extreme, but there’s a Grecian grandeur to McDonagh’s tale that emerges in the telling. Farrell and Gleeson bounce off one another superbly, Kerry Condon is magnificent as Siobhán, Pádraic’s exasperated sister, and Barry Keoghan is a wide-eyed young islander who may not be quite the ‘gom’ he seems. McDonagh’s best film yet, by some distance.‘Based on James Joyce’s long short story, John Huston’s sublime swan song chronicles the events at a Dublin party thrown to mark the Feast of the Epiphany in 1904. Through this commonplace gathering, Joyce (and Huston) explores universal themes of love, longing and loss’ Michael Doherty on The DeadAnjelica Huston and Donal McCann in The Dead10 The Dead (1987)OK, so John Huston wasn’t Irish, but he had a house here, and was dying himself (of emphysema) while he shot his last film, a loving adaptation of James Joyce’s elegiac short story. The great Donal McCann, who would be dead within a decade or so himself, was never better than as Gabriel Conroy, who on a snowy night in January 1904, goes to his aunts’ house on Usher’s Island for a party. With him goes his beautiful wife Gretta (Anjelica Huston), and amid the stories, songs and rows over nationalism and Charles Stewart Parnell, Gabriel’s simmering unhappiness becomes evident.He loves his wife, but is jealous of a dead man, a boy she loved long ago and is now buried under the falling snow in Galway.Huston was so sick he directed the film from a wheelchair and regularly paused to suck oxygen. But it’s among his very best works, so much so that even that old sourpuss Pauline Kael of the New Yorker was impressed.A sombre masterpiece.9 In the Name of the Father (1993)Part of a remarkable series of collaborations between Jim Sheridan and Daniel Day-Lewis, this lean thriller was based on the true and tragic story of Gerry Conlon and the Guildford Four. Young Belfast tearaway Conlon is sent to London by his father Giuseppe after he gets in trouble with the IRA. But in the hysteria that followed the Guildford pub bombings, Conlon, his friend Paul Hill and two others are arrested and tortured into making false confessions.The nightmare gets worse for Gerry when his father is arrested and charged as well, and they end up in the same prison. Day-Lewis lost 25kg to play the role, and mastered the hard music of the Belfast accent perfectly. His scenes with Pete Postlethwaite, who plays Giuseppe, are very moving. Both received Oscar nods, and the film was nominated for seven in total.‘Michael Collins is our own historical epic. Annual reruns and mandatory watching at school might have jaded people to its quality but it’s a quintessential Irish film and cultural document by one of the all-time great Irish directors’ Will Fitzgerald on Michael CollinsLiam Neeson in the title role in Michael Collins8 Michael Collins (1996)It was quite a thing, back in the mid-1990s, to sit in the Savoy Cinema on O’Connell Street and watch Neil Jordan’s epic recreation of the battle for the GPO. Inside the building’s gutted shell hide Michael Collins (Liam Neeson) and his old friend Harry Boland (Aidan Quinn), who vow to fight on. “We won’t play by their rules Harry,” Collins vows darkly, “we’ll invent our own.” The film then documents Collins’ brilliant and ruthless guerilla campaign, the Anglo-Irish Treaty negotiations, the falling-out with Éamon de Valera (an excellent Alan Rickman) and Collins’ death at Béal na Bláth.“The minute I announced that I was going into production on it,” Jordan told me a few years back, “everyone began arguing. It was almost like I’d been commissioned to make a national monument or something”. Though not everyone loved Julia Roberts’ Kitty Kiernan, Jordan did a great job.‘It cuts through to the repression of rural Ireland of the 1960s, the impossibility of family life and the masquerade of the church with compassion and deep, black humour’ Ruth Barton on The Butcher Boy7 The Butcher Boy (1997)Neil Jordan’s unflinching adaptation of Patrick McCabe’s novel was at the top of several of our judges’ lists, and retains a special fascination for those of us who remember Ireland in the bad old days. In Clones, Co Monaghan, in the early 1960s, 12-year-old Francie Brady (Eamonn Owens) retreats regularly into a TV and movie-inspired fantasy world. When his mother dies by suicide, he ends up in the tender care of his bad-tempered alcoholic father. And things get even worse when he is sent to reform school and molested by a priest.Jordan blends elaborate dream sequences with the brutal realities of Francie’s unravelling life exceptionally well, and those visions of a swearing Virgin Mary (memorably played by a perfectly cast Sinéad O’Connor) felt like an angry statement about our theocratic past.Daniel Day-Lewis in My Left Foot6 My Left Foot (1989)Jim Sheridan’s debut feature was a massive shot in the arm for our then tiny film industry, and was the first properly Irish movie to make a massive international splash. Nominated for five Academy Awards, winner of two, My Left Foot put us well and truly on the cinematic map, and set the stage for future Irish Oscar triumphs, which would become less and less rare. Daniel Day-Lewis announced himself as one of the great screen actors of his generation playing Christy Brown, a working-class Dubliner who overcame cerebral palsy to become a celebrated artist and writer.Day-Lewis famously went full-on method during the production, staying in the wheelchair between takes and having to be lifted over cables — and even fed — by the forbearing crew. Which sounds extreme, but without all that, would his Christy have been quite as good?5 The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006)Directed by an Englishman, written by a Scot, Ken Loach’s epic was considered eligible by our panel because of its subject matter, and an almost entirely Irish cast. Cillian Murphy plays Damien O’Donovan, a young man who is about to leave Cork to practise medicine in a London hospital as the War of Independence gathers pace. His brother Teddy (Pádraic Delaney) commands the local flying column, but Damien believes it’s a war that can’t be won. But when Teddy is captured and tortured by the Black and Tans, and another friend is shot dead for refusing to say his name in English, Damien relents and takes up arms himself.Loach and his writer Paul Laverty, both staunch anti-imperialists, give us an outsider’s view of the Irish struggle for independence, which would become such a beacon of hope for other budding nations across the globe. But for Irish audiences, whose history had so rarely been dramatised, watching a flying column in action was an awesome sight.‘The understated beauty and bittersweet familiarity of small-town Ireland comes of age in the hands of master craftsman Lenny Abrahamson. Pat Shortt’s performance is a revelation.’ Dearbhla Walsh on GarageAnne-Marie Duff and Pat Shortt in Garage4 Garage (2007)One of two Lenny Abrahamson films on our list, this little gem of a feature written by Mark O’Halloran offers a bleak and unsentimental insight into life in small-town Ireland. Giving the performance of his life, Pat Shortt plays the central role of Josie, a simple-minded but sunny-natured attendant at a crumbling rural garage. He lives in a squalid room at the back, and endures the jeers of the regulars at the local pub, but is more or less contented with his lot.His equilibrium is disturbed when a teenage boy arrives to help out at the garage, but Josie’s warmth soon wins him over, and they become friends. But a misunderstanding over an adult video brings the town down on Josie’s head. With beautifully spare dialogue from O’Halloran, wistful direction from Abrahamson and a subtle but powerful performance from Shortt, Garage is a simple, sombre and very moving drama.‘Iconic, fun, and generous of spirit, just like its director, Alan Parker, who showed me great professional kindness when I was starting out’ Fiona Clark on The CommitmentsMaria Doyle Kennedy and Angeline Ball and in The Commitments3 The Commitments (1991)The first of a series of films based on the novels of Roddy Doyle, Alan Parker’s 1991 film had a huge impact both at home and abroad, and captured in a sense what it is to be from Dublin. Robert Arkins was Jimmy Rabbitte, a would-be impresario with big ambitions who forms a soul band with several of his old schoolfriends. After holding auditions for singers, he calls the band The Commitments and turns them into a formidable rhythm and blues outfit that gains a big reputation belting out soul standards from Otis Redding and Wilson Pickett. But internal pressures and an obnoxious lead singer cause a disaster just as they are about to land a record deal.Watching this film as an emigrant was a very special feeling because, for the first time perhaps, a recognisable version of the Ireland we grew up in was appearing on the screen. Which perhaps explains why The Commitments has a special place in many Irish hearts.‘Lenny Abrahamson’s visionary and beautiful film made a huge impact on me when it came out, and it’s still my favourite Irish movie’ Frank Berry on Adam & PaulTom Murphy and Mark O'Halloran in Adam & Paul 2 Adam & Paul (2004)Lenny Abrahamson joined forces with writer Mark O’Halloran to create Adam & Paul, a funny, absurd and tragic odyssey following the desperate exploits of a pair of Dublin heroin addicts. It was unlike any Irish film before it, and displayed a rare visual aesthetic in a country prone to verbiage. O’Halloran was Adam, a Dublin drug addict who trawls the city streets daily looking for the next score in the company of his childhood friend Paul (Tom Murphy).Their hapless search for an unnamed contact reminded critics of Waiting for Godot, and the broad jokes were mixed with scenes of incredible pathos — who could forget the moment when Adam and Paul end up minding a friend’s baby. It remains an unforgettable movie, and one wonders what Tom Murphy might have achieved had he not died so tragically just three years later, at the age of 39.Adam & Paul was the Irish film that changed everything.‘An overwhelmingly beautiful piece of cinema. A very Irish story, told with such artistry and skill that it resonated around the world’ Sinéad Egan on An Cailín CiúinCatherine Clinch in An Cailín Ciúin 1 An Cailín Ciúin (2022)Based on Claire Keegan’s story Foster, Colm Bairéad’s quiet, lyrical drama snuck into Irish cinemas in May 2022, giving little indication of the massive impact it would have. Numerous international awards and an Oscar nomination later, its status as one of the best Irish films ever made seems assured. Written and directed by Bairéad, and produced by Cleona Ní Chrualaoí, An Cailín Ciúin addresses as Gaeilge the themes of childhood, grief and loneliness in spare and unsentimental fashion, and provides an insight into a recent but very different Ireland in which children were numerous, and consequently undervalued.Catherine Clinch plays Cáit, a quiet, pensive nine-year-old girl whose overwrought mother is expecting yet another child. It’s 1981, and as the birth looms, Cáit is deemed surplus to requirements and sent to live with her mother’s cousin, Eibhlín (Carrie Crowley).Eibhlín and her husband Seán (Andrew Bennett) have no children, and are strangers to Cáit, who is all at sea in a strange house and might expect the worst. Instead, she finds kindness, calmness and a loving understanding she has never previously experienced.As it was only released last year, An Cailín Ciúin is fresh in our minds and so might be expected to feature prominently here.
